name: Burnt Umber
lede: Burnt umber is the reddish brown made by roasting umber, the manganese-rich earth whose name most likely means shadow; painters have used it for deep, translucent shadows since the 1500s.

sections.title: What the name says
sections.body:
Burnt umber is raw [[umber]] that has been roasted, and the name says exactly that [1][9]. Paterson defines it as a reddish-brown pigment made by treating umber with fire, and lists it among the dictionary's browns beside burnt ochre and burnt sienna [9]. The word *umber* most likely comes from the Latin *ombra*, shadow, since this was the pigment painters reached for to build shadows, and not from Umbria in Italy [2][3][5]. Ball adds that European umber was imported mostly from Turkey, which weakens the Umbria link further [3].

This page is about the roasted pigment and the swatch. The raw earth, its minerals and its mines are told on the [[umber]] page.

sections.title: What roasting does
sections.body:
Raw umber is a fine-grained rock of manganese and iron oxides and hydroxides [2]. Heating it in air drives water out of the iron hydroxides and converts them to iron oxide, so the pigment turns a "warm reddish brown" in Weber's 1923 words while keeping raw umber's usefulness as a drier in oil [1]. The change is the same one that turns yellow ochre orange and then red, a point Coles makes about burnt ochres generally [7].

Manganese stays in the mix, and it is what keeps burnt umber darker than its neighbor [[sienna]] after roasting [3][7]. Jarman, who points out that brown is not in the spectrum, lists its pigments as earth brown, burnt umber, burnt ochre and burnt sienna [6]. All are earths cooked to red heat, and he remarks that cooking is present in brown [6]. Gurney's table of modern pigments lists burnt umber under the Colour Index code PBr 7, a code it shares with burnt sienna, so the name labels a material class and not a single recipe [8].

sections.title: The first burnt umber
sections.body:
Ball says umber reached European painting near the end of the fifteenth century [3]. The roasted form was valued for deep but translucent shadows [3]. Our archive of paintings, which sees only colors and not pigments, finds the brown peaking in the 1400s (see the field notes) [13].

Documents are blurrier than the pigment. Harley found that English sources of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries largely ignore the difference between raw and burnt umber, and she argues that an unqualified "umber" often meant the burnt kind, which was the more widely used [1]. The painter Edward Norgate described umber as bought as a foul, greasy color that was cleaned by burning it in a crucible [1]. Ball quotes the same remark and places it in the 1620s, while the Compendium dates Norgate's discourse to 1648 to 1650, so the books disagree on when he wrote [1][3]. Both agree on his practical point: burnt umber was hard to grind and work as bought, yet very useful for shadows and hair [3].

sections.title: Cyprus, Turkey and the others
sections.body:
The best umber came from Cyprus, and Terry in 1893 called the Margi deposit west of Nicosia the darkest and richest, a warm violet brown [2]. Dealers wrote of "Turkey umber" or "Turkish umber", because Anatolia was not distinguished from Cyprus in the eighteenth century, and Church lists a Levant umber [2]. Terry complained that the English umbers of Derbyshire were gritty and reddish [2]. In Ireland the reddish Cappagh brown, which Weber says was mined in Cork in 1814, was an umber of the English type, and it was later imitated by mixing peat or bitumen with burnt umber and burnt sienna [2][10].

So a nineteenth-century tube of burnt umber could come from a Cyprus quarry, a Derbyshire pit or a factory mix [2][10]. The name, as the Compendium says of umber terminology in general, is a minefield [2].

sections.title: Burnt umber inside other colors
sections.body:
Burnt umber was also an ingredient. The Compendium records recipes in which it appears as a base: Fishwick's Devonshire brown combined it with Frankfort black, rose pink and colcothar [10]. Terra cotta, as Mayer lists it, was burnt umber with a natural red iron oxide and chalk, with baryte, zinc oxide or lithopone replacing the chalk [10]. Toch said Verona brown was a fancy name for burnt umber with burnt or raw sienna, and Mayer's fawn brown and velvet brown mix raw or burnt umber with dark ochre [10]. Mayer lists jacaranta brown, euchrome and mineral brown as synonyms for it, though Salter says the last two were trade names for Cappagh brown [10].

The practical lesson for a reader of old recipes is that a color called brown, terra cotta or fawn was often a burnt umber with something added [10].

sections.title: Not to be confused with Cassel earth
sections.body: Pigments sold as Cassel, Cologne or Kassel "umber" belong with the lignite brown better known as Vandyke brown, and are misnomers if applied to true umbers [2][10]. Ball describes Cassel earth as an organic material from peat or lignite, not a mineral, with early sources near the German cities of Cologne and Cassel [3]. Vandyke brown took the name of the painter [[painter:anthony-van-dyck|Anthony van Dyck]] in English from about 1790 [3]. If a seventeenth-century source says "Cologne umber", it may mean this one [2][3].

sections.title: In painting
sections.body:
Brown has never had good press. St Clair notes that because brown is a shade and not a hue, medieval artists saw it as corrupt, and Pissarro claimed to banish earth pigments from his palette [5]. Yet earth browns, ochers, umber, bister, sinopia and Cassel earth built the shadows of the baroque [5]. Ball calls Correggio, Caravaggio and Rembrandt the masters of black and brown, and writes that nothing matches the profundity of umber for a sombre palette [3].

Rembrandt is the best documented case. By the 1650s he used about half a dozen mostly earthy pigments, among them ochres, siennas and umbers, and they have aged well because he knew what was stable [4]. After his bankruptcy in 1656, St Clair says, he leaned on cheap ochers, umber above all, for the dark surroundings and cloth in his late self-portraits [5]. For [[painter:rembrandt-van-rijn|Rembrandt]] the brown was not dirt; it was the space around the face [5].

St Clair also names Caravaggio's *Nativity* of 1609, which she describes as a very dark scene with figures picked out against a muddy ground that probably owed its darkness to umber, and the painting was stolen from Palermo in 1969 and is lost [5]. That makes it an attractive example and an unusable one. Treat umber in [[painter:caravaggio|Caravaggio]] as a plausible attribution, not a measured one [5].

sections.title: The swatch is not the pigment
sections.body:
The swatch here, `#8A3324`, is a strong reddish brown, closer to brick than to an umber tube [11]. Our library also holds Ridgway's burnt umber, `#6C5043`, a duller grayish brown, and the xkcd survey's version, `#A0450E`, a rust orange [11]. All three are called burnt umber, and they are far apart [11]. The name appears in our sources from Ridgway's 1886 nomenclature, then Ridgway again in 1912, and ISCC-NBS in 1955, which is a late date for a color that had been on palettes for centuries [11].

The nearest named color in the library, Kobe, `#882D17`, lists Burnt Umber among its alternate names and has a Maerz and Paul entry of 1924 [11]. Pigment hexes are screen approximations, and a real tube is darker and changes with the binder [11].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, this swatch appears in 1,145 (4.81 per cent), and in 1,100 by the stricter within-painting count [12]. That is more common than 91 per cent of the named colors [12]. Inside a painting it is an accent in 87 per cent of those 1,100, which fits a color used for glazes and darks [12].

It peaks in the 1400s, when 148 of 945 paintings (15.7 per cent) hold it, 3.1 times the museums' baseline [12]. Among painters with many works, Botticelli carries it in 10 of 48 [12], and Dürer in 8 of 47 [12]. Tibet is the most over-represented place, 9 of 47 paintings [12]. The first dated painting that holds it at least 2 per cent of the canvas is from 1150 (cma-135486), which is a floor and not a first, and 736 years before the earliest record of the name in our sources [12].

The same caveat as every archive number holds: these are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a brown that old varnish has darkened counts the same as a brown a painter chose [12].

origin.first_recorded: English documents of the 1500s and 1600s often mean it by plain "umber"; Norgate, 1620s or 1648-50 (books disagree); the color name in our sources from Ridgway 1886

questions.q: How is burnt umber made from raw umber?
choices: By roasting it, which turns iron hydroxides into iron oxide
By mixing it with bone black
questions.answer: By roasting it, which turns iron hydroxides into iron oxide

Why can an old recipe that says only "umber" be hard to read?
choices: English sources often ignored the raw/burnt distinction, and plain umber often meant burnt
The word was used only for Cassel earth

openers: Burnt umber is raw umber roasted until its iron hydroxides turn to oxide, which shifts it from olive-brown to reddish brown.
Three swatches all called burnt umber (a brick red, a grayish brown and a rust orange) sit in our library: the name is wider than any one hex.
Look for burnt umber in the dark ground around a face, as in Rembrandt's late self-portraits.
